blocks.text: The discovery of cells, and then the further study of the internal structure of cells, depended on the use of the microscope. Microscopy is the technique of using microscopes to observe and study objects that are too small to be seen with the naked eye. Microscopes use lenses and light or electron beams to magnify and illuminate specimens.

In a light microscope, light is used to make the image of the object. Light passes through the object and then through two glass lenses. One lens produces an enlarged image of the object and the second lens magnifies the image more. After passing through the object and the lenses, the light forms an enlarged, clear image of the object in the viewer's eye.

blocks.alt: (a) A compound light microscope with its parts labelled: eyepiece (ocular lens), arm, nosepiece, objective lens, specimen on the stage, diaphragm, coarse adjustment, fine adjustment, light source and base. (b) The working principle: light from the source passes up through the condenser, the specimen, the objective lens and the ocular lens to the viewer's eye.

blocks.text: These are the two key characteristics of microscopes.

blocks.title: Magnification
blocks.text: A microscope's ability to enlarge the image of an object. Different lenses offer different levels of magnification. It is denoted by the symbol X, which tells how many times larger the image appears compared to the actual size: a 10X lens enlarges a 1 µm object to 10 µm. Total magnification is found by multiplying the magnifications of all the lenses.

blocks.title: Resolution
blocks.text: A microscope's ability to distinguish between two points that are close together on an object. The greater the resolution, the finer the detail that can be observed. The naked human eye resolves about 0.1 mm; a light microscope resolves details down to approximately 250 nm.

The magnification of a light microscope is 1500X: it can magnify objects about 1500 times. Its resolving power is 0.2 micrometre (µm), where 1 µm is one thousandth of a millimetre. In other words, the light microscope cannot distinguish objects smaller than 0.2 µm.

Light microscopes are advantageous for viewing living organisms, but since individual cells are generally transparent, their components are not distinguishable unless they are coloured with special stains (coloured chemicals). Staining, however, usually kills the cells.

In an electron microscope, a beam of electrons passes through the object. Magnetic lenses focus the electron beam onto a screen or photographic film and make a much enlarged image. Its resolving power is much greater than that of a light microscope: it can clearly show objects as small as 0.2 nanometre (nm), where 1 nm is one millionth of a millimetre. However, an electron microscope cannot be used to view living material, because of the methods needed to prepare the specimens. Biologists use two types of electron microscope.

items: Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM): used to view the internal structure of a cell. A TEM transmits a beam of electrons through a very thin specimen. It can magnify objects up to 250,000 times.

Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM): used to study the details of the surfaces of cells or other objects. The surfaces are coated with metal; when the electron beam hits the metal it is reflected and makes an enlarged image. SEMs magnify up to 100,000 times.

blocks.alt: (a) Scanning electron microscope: an electron source at the top, condenser lenses, an aperture, a scanning coil and the objective lens focus a fine beam onto the sample; a back-scattered electron detector and a secondary electron detector collect electrons from the sample, and the signal passes through an amplifier, with a scan generator, to a computer screen.

blocks.long_description: (a) Scanning electron microscope: an electron source at the top, condenser lenses, an aperture, a scanning coil and the objective lens focus a fine beam onto the sample; a back-scattered electron detector and a secondary electron detector collect electrons from the sample, and the signal passes through an amplifier, with a scan generator, to a computer screen. (b) Transmission electron microscope: electron source, condenser lenses, condenser aperture, sample, objective lens, objective aperture, intermediate lenses, projective lens, and a fluorescent screen and camera at the bottom.
